name: Bubonic plague (flea- and louse-borne, as in the Second Pandemic)

reproduction_number_range.source: Dean et al. 2018, PNAS, doi 10.1073/pnas.1715640115, full text at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5819418 (opened): the human-ectoparasite model gives an estimated R0 from 1.48 (Eyam) to 1.91 (Barcelona) across nine pre-industrial outbreaks (Table 3 and Results); the pneumonic and rat-flea model variants give other ranges and are not used here

transmissibility_per_day.source: The midpoint of the sourced reproduction number range (1.695) divided by the infectious days, rounded

case_fatality.source: WHO plague fact sheet, who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague: 'a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 60% for the bubonic type'; 0.45 is the midpoint (the page gives no untreated qualifier for that range)

immunity.source: Madagascar plague patients (PMC7653777, opened): anti-F1 antibody 'could persist for more than a decade in both BP and PP recovered patients', one patient seropositive at 14.8 years, which the authors say 'suggests its probable involvement in patients' protection'; the paper does not report reinfections. A Chinese cohort of 65 survivors over 16 years reported no reinfection (search summary only, not opened). Lifelong immunity is therefore a ballpark, a decade or more is read; Dean et al. 2018 (PMC5819418) say their models ignore immunity.

stage.incubating.source: WHO plague fact sheet: 'an incubation period of one to seven days'; the 4 day mean is the midpoint. Shape 4 is a middling spread, not sourced

stage.infectious.source: Dean et al. 2018 (PMC5819418, Table 2): an average duration of infection of 10 days for bubonic plague in humans in the rat-flea model (the human-ectoparasite model splits it into 8 mildly and 2 highly infectious days, the same 10 total). Shape 2 is a broad spread, not sourced

density_exponent.source: Wikipedia, Basic reproduction number (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_reproduction_number, opened): R0 = contact rate / recovery rate, the contact rate set by 'the number of susceptible people in the population that the infected people contact'; whether contact rises with density is not stated there. Chowell et al., 1918 influenza in England and Wales (PMC2596813, opened): 'we found no association between transmissibility, death rates and indicators of population density and residential crowding', R between 1.3 and 1.9, and deaths scaling as population to the power 0.71-0.77 in rural areas and about 1.0 in towns. So the exponent of contact on crowding lies between 0 (that study) and 1 (mass action, density-dependent contact); 0.5 is the midpoint, a ballpark. Rader et al. 2020 (Nature Medicine; search summary only, full text not opened): crowded cities have longer epidemics and larger attack rates.
